body: Carney’s remarks offer modest support for the Canadian dollar, as any easing of the 50% US tariff would lift a weight on Canadian exporters and the growth outlook. The lack of a timeline limits how much a trade-deal premium can build, so USD/CAD is likely to stay more sensitive to the US midterm results and oil prices in the near term. Canada is the largest foreign supplier of crude to the US, so a broader settlement would also reduce one source of uncertainty for North American energy flows. Sectors hit by Canada’s counter-tariffs, including US steel, dairy and farm equipment exporters, stand to gain most if talks succeed. Carney is sounding more optimistic about a US trade deal than at any point since talks collapsed in August, but he is careful not to promise one. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said trade discussions with the United States will become more intensive. He reported progress in the talks while cautioning that important areas remain unresolved and a deal is not yet done. Carney said some of the red lines in the negotiations had been removed, but others still needed to be addressed. He described the shift in Washington’s position as the United States asking for less and offering more, while stressing that the two sides were not there yet. He also played down the need for formal negotiating rounds. He said it was not always necessary for Canadian trade negotiators to be talking directly with the Office of the US Trade Representative, because good lines of communication were open between the two governments. The comments build on Carney’s update over the weekend, when he said he had held a good conversation with President Donald Trump. He said then that teams from both countries would work over the coming weeks on the outlines of a deal. Trump said last week that he expected a new agreement pretty soon, without giving details. The talks are trying to repair a relationship that deteriorated sharply in August, when negotiations broke down. Trump then imposed a 50% tariff on around $20bn of Canadian goods, equal to roughly 5.5% of Canada’s exports. Ottawa responded with matching tariffs on US products including steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics. Carney’s tone is notably more upbeat than at any point since that breakdown, but his remarks were careful to avoid suggesting an agreement was imminent. His repeated references to unresolved areas and remaining red lines suggest the hardest issues are still on the table, and he gave no timeline for a final deal. The timing adds a political dimension. Americans vote in midterm elections on Tuesday, and trade tensions with Canada are a live issue in states such as Michigan and Maine. The outcome could shape how much room the White House has to compromise in the weeks ahead. body: The miss on every major measure is likely to weigh on the New Zealand dollar and trim pricing for a December rate hike. The kiwi was already near a cycle low against the Australian dollar after last week’s RBNZ hold, and the gap with a more hawkish RBA now looks set to widen. The weak jobs figures argue against tightening, but the RBNZ’s hawks have focused on core inflation and fuel costs. A labour market miss alone may not settle the debate, so inflation expectations surveys later this month carry extra weight. Front-end swap rates are the market to watch for how far hike bets are pared. --- Banks called the peak in New Zealand unemployment, but the labour market went the other way, and the RBNZ’s December hike now looks a harder sell. New Zealand’s unemployment rate rose to 5.7% in the third quarter, above expectations of 5.5%, as employment unexpectedly fell and wage growth slowed, data from Statistics New Zealand showed on Wednesday. Employment declined 0.1% from the previous quarter, against a Reuters poll forecast of a 0.4% gain. The participation rate dropped to 70.4% from 70.6%, below the 70.7% expected. Unemployment rose even though fewer people were looking for work, which points to weak hiring rather than a growing labour force. Earlier figures were also revised lower, with second-quarter employment growth cut to 0.3% from 0.5%. The result runs against bank forecasts that had pointed to a peak in joblessness. Westpac had expected the rate to ease to 5.5%, while ANZ had forecast no change at 5.6%. The June quarter reading of 5.6% was already the highest since 2015. Wage pressures also eased. Private sector wages excluding overtime rose 0.4% in the quarter, below the 0.5% expected, taking annual growth to 2.0% from 2.1%. The data lands at a sensitive moment for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. On 28 October it held the official cash rate at 2.75% in a 4:3 vote, surprising markets that had largely priced a hike. The majority cited weaker than expected inflation, stable inflation expectations and subdued wage growth, and argued that two earlier rate increases needed time to work. Wednesday’s figures support that case on both jobs and pay. Westpac had described today’s release as the first key input before the RBNZ’s next decision on 9 December, while still forecasting a hike at that meeting. The bank cautioned that the move was not a done deal, and a weaker labour market makes that case harder to argue. New Zealand holds a general election on Saturday, adding further uncertainty to the policy outlook ahead of the December meeting. There's always something new to learn about the markets. title: Iran War Doubles Egypt’s LNG Bill as Gas Output Keeps Falling
summary: The war on Iran has doubled what Egypt pays for imported LNG, and Cairo is deferring cargoes into 2027 and burning fuel oil in its power plants to hold down the bill. QatarEnergy has kept its LNG deliveries under force majeure since April, and on October 28 it extended…
body: Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. The war on Iran has doubled what Egypt pays for imported LNG, and Cairo is deferring cargoes into 2027 and burning fuel oil in its power plants to hold down the bill. Egypt’s own output fell to 3.63 bcf/d in August as older fields declined faster than new wells came online, and the petroleum ministry has now extended the deadline for bids on 14 exploration blocks meant to reverse that decline to December 14 after companies asked for more time. QatarEnergy has kept its LNG deliveries under force majeure since April, and on October 28 it extended that to the end of December. A government official told Asharq Bloomberg that the price of a single LNG cargo has risen as much as 100% since September, to more than $100 million. Cairo has asked suppliers to push five of its 15 November LNG cargoes into 2027, on top of about 15 cargoes it had already deferred since July. The Petroleum Ministry budgeted $10.1 billion for LNG imports in the fiscal year that began July 1 and had spent $5.8 billion of it by October 6. Egypt has set aside about $1 billion for November cargoes. To cut the bill, EGPC bought six cargoes of high-sulfur fuel oil for delivery in November and December. Egypt’s fuel oil imports have trended higher since April and exceeded 640,000 tons in October. Egyptian gas output has fallen steadily since late 2021. It averaged 4.87 bcf/d in 2024 , then an eight-year low, and about 4 bcf/d in the second half of 2025. In July, Egypt imported more gas than it produced for the first time on record. Imports eased to 3.44 bcf/d in August, still almost half of what the country consumes: 2.24 bcf/d of LNG and 1.20 bcf/d by pipeline from Israel, whose Leviathan partners hold a $35 billion agreement to raise exports to Egypt through 2040. Existing fields lose about 120 mmcfd of output each month, according to the Asharq Bloomberg report. Kpler says new wells and Shell’s (NYSE:SHEL) Mina West field may hold production flat in early 2027 before the decline resumes. Related: IEA Warns Global Gas Crunch Could Last Well into 2027 Petroleum Minister Karim Badawi pledged on September 16 to add about 330 mmcfd of domestic gas by the end of 2026: about 250 mmcfd from the Zohr and West Mina fields in the Mediterranean and about 80 mmcfd from Meleiha in the Western Desert, which he had due by end-September. Eni’s (NYSE:E) Nidoco N-2 well in the Nile Delta started producing about 55 mmcfd in July. BP (NYSE:BP) brought the Fayoum-4 well online in the West Nile Delta on August 31 at about 80 mmcfd, nearly two years early, by drilling sideways from an existing well. Agiba Petroleum, Eni’s joint venture with EGPC, began start-up of the 100 mmcfd Meleiha Phase 2 plant on October 20, three weeks past Badawi’s deadline. Shell’s Mina West field, at about 120 mmcfd, is due to start before year-end. On October 24, the petroleum ministry announced that Chevron’s (NYSE:CVX) Nargis-2 appraisal well in the Mediterranean had encountered up to 35 metres of net gas pay. The well was drilled to more than 5,000 metres, confirmed an extension of the previously discovered reservoir and found an additional gas-bearing layer. MEES estimated the original Nargis discovery, announced in December 2022, at about 3.5 tcf. Chevron operates the concession with 45%, alongside Eni with 30%, Mubadala Energy with 15% and Tharwa Petroleum with 10%. Mubadala bought its stake from Eni in February. On October 5, Chevron signed for the deepwater Lotus block, committing at least $88 million to two exploration wells in 2,000 to 2,800 metres of water, where no deep exploratory well has been drilled. Egypt made nine discoveries in the fiscal year to June, adding about 2.8 tcf of gas reserves. In July, the petroleum ministry announced a find at the Watda deep well in the Western Desert, which Khalda Petroleum, the joint venture of Apache and EGPC, tested at about 40 mmcfd. title: Global Diesel Crunch Set to Last Well Into 2027
summary: While crude oil imports in Asia have reached pre-war levels, imports of refined products remain weak as gasoline and diesel imports from the Middle East have crashed amid reduced refining capacity. Asia’s oil import story these days is a reflection of the global oil markets—crude oil availability has significantly increased since the early summer lows and flows out of the Middle East have largely recovered, but supply of gasoline, and especially diesel, has sharply dropped since the Iran war began at the end of February. Reduced refinery…
body: What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… While crude oil imports in Asia have reached pre-war levels, imports of refined products remain weak as gasoline and diesel imports from the Middle East have crashed amid reduced refining capacity. Asia’s oil import story these days is a reflection of the global oil markets—crude oil availability has significantly increased since the early summer lows and flows out of the Middle East have largely recovered, but supply of gasoline, and especially diesel, has sharply dropped since the Iran war began at the end of February. Reduced refinery runs in the Middle East, with some refineries still out following Iranian strikes in the early days of the war, have combined with lower refined product flows through the Strait of Hormuz, due to the much more dangerous ship-to-ship transfers of highly inflammable fuels, to slash supply to the market. Russia’s fuel crunch due to Ukrainian strikes on refineries and the lack of Russian diesel exports have compounded the global diesel problem, sending refining margins and retail prices to record highs in the third quarter of the year. The crunch is extending into the fourth quarter, and could last well into 2027, analysts say, as many refineries will have to undergo in the spring long overdue maintenance that has been deferred from this year to maximize production. In this context, crude and product imports in Asia, the world’s biggest oil-importing region, are telling of the state of the global oil market. Asia’s crude oil imports jumped to 26.39 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, up from 24.24 million bpd the month prior, per data by Kpler cited by Reuters’ Asia Commodities and Energy Columnist Clyde Russell. The import levels are estimated at nearly par with the three-month average of 27 million bpd before the Iran war, and up by 39% compared to the lowest level during the conflict so far of 19 million bpd in April, according to the data. Related: IEA Warns Global Gas Crunch Could Last Well into 2027 Asia’s crude imports that have moved through the Strait of Hormuz soared to 7.4 million bpd in October, compared to just 1.6 million bpd in April. Flows through Hormuz en route to Asia are still lagging the pre-war levels of about 13 million bpd, but supply has jumped from Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea port of Yanbu. In recent months, Asian refiners have also materially raised crude oil imports from Russia and the Americas to offset the supply lost at the Strait of Hormuz. In contrast, Asia’s light and middle distillate imports, estimated at about 6.15 million bpd in October by Kpler, were still 10% below pre-war levels. Imports from the Middle East alone remain 18.4% below pre-war volumes, although Asia’s total fuel imports rose from September on the back of increased supply from the Americas and Africa. Gasoline and especially diesel supply remains more restricted than crude oil flows. Since the summer, diesel has been the most distressed barrel in the oil market and soaring refining margins and wholesale and retail prices globally are reflecting this constraint. Despite the recovered crude flows, refineries outside the Middle East and Russia cannot offset the lost capacity, at a time when diesel and other middle distillate demand is rising going into the northern hemisphere winter. China’s near-term export policies will be key for Asia’s regional supply in the fourth quarter, analysts say. “China remains the main Asian uncertainty. October’s clean-product export plan was around 500 kt below September’s, while November diesel and jet export volumes remain unclear,” Abhishek Kumar, senior oil market analyst at Sparta Commodities, said last week. “Additional Chinese cargoes could loosen Asian balances, but the market needs greater clarity on approvals and actual loadings.” For global supply, the crunch is likely to extend unt

title: Big Oil Puts Debt Reduction Ahead of New Investments
summary: The world’s biggest oil and gas companies have posted another strong quarter, with just Europe’s top six majors booking a collective $38 billion for the July-to-September quarter. Adding Exxon and Chevron, the figure swells considerably. But the supermajors are in no rush to start spending that windfall. The oil and gas industry is having the exact opposite year to 2020. The war between the United States and Israel, and Iran has pushed oil and gas prices to the highest in years. The war between Russia and Ukraine, meanwhile, has driven…
body: What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… The world’s biggest oil and gas companies have posted another strong quarter, with just Europe’s top six majors booking a collective $38 billion for the July-to-September quarter. Adding Exxon and Chevron, the figure swells considerably. But the supermajors are in no rush to start spending that windfall. The oil and gas industry is having the exact opposite year to 2020. The war between the United States and Israel, and Iran has pushed oil and gas prices to the highest in years. The war between Russia and Ukraine, meanwhile, has driven refining margins to all-time highs, adding to refining disruption in the Middle East. The combination of developments has driven Exxon’s third-quarter profit up twofold from a year ago, Chevron has booked triple the profit it booked for last year’s third quarter, and BP has reported its highest quarterly profit in its long history. Normally, with these formidable profits, Big Oil should be looking for ways to spend it. Analysts call it a supercycle, and supercycles drive super investments. Not this time, however. This time, Big Oil appears to be focusing on paying down debt, repurchasing stock, and being picky about new investments. Indeed, BP even suspended its share buyback program to cut debt faster—and it has, slashing the total by as much as $10 billion, with the remaining pile now at $13.9 billion. Big Oil appears to be approaching its strong year with a sober mind. Some observers believe this approach to extra-large profits is a sign that Big Oil remains wary of the long-term prospects for their industry. Reuters’ Ron Bousso wrote in a column this week that “Big Oil has so far shied away from major new spending, suggesting the majors do not see today’s market conditions as evidence that the industry’s long-term outlook has improved.” Related: IEA Warns Global Gas Crunch Could Last Well into 2027 This is an interesting suggestion. It would be safe to say that Big Oil companies are quite aware of the fact that the market environment this year is far from the ordinary. It would also be safe to say they are unlikely to be complacent and believe the windfall will never end because that would be childishly naïve, and these are not words one tends to associate with the oil industry. However, the long-term outlook for oil and gas is arguably brighter than it was, say, two years ago. Because the war and its effect on the global economy has demonstrated unequivocally that despite the massive transition push of the past decade, hydrocarbons remain the dominant fuel globally. Not all agree within the industry itself. TotalEnergies, for instance, recently revised its peak oil demand forecast, now expecting that peak between 2035 and 2040. Previously, the company had expected demand to peak after 2040. On the other hand, back in 2024, TotalEnergies expected oil demand to peak after 2030. Meanwhile, commodity trading major Vitol has forecast that oil demand will continue growing until 2040, citing slower than expected global adoption of electric vehicles. Electric vehicles—the electrification of transport—is widely accepted as the leading factor for oil demand decline in the future. It is quite likely the reason Big Oil is being smart with its extra profits this year and not doing business as usual, splurging when the going is good and tightening belts when the cycle hits the trough Still, many forecasts about mass EV adoption and peaking oil demand within a few years turned out to be very far from reality, including a prediction by the International Energy Agency that oil, gas, and coal demand will all start declining before 2030. Big Oil may well be preparing for a long-term future with weaker overall oil and gas demand. body: Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… The American Petroleum Institute (API) estimated that crude oil inventories in the United States fell by 5.267 million barrels in the week ending October 30. In the week prior, US crude oil inventories fell by a staggering 2.031 million barrels. Commercial crude oil inventories excluding the SPR have lost more than 64 million barrels over the last 29 weeks, and 12 million over this year, according to API data, which has been kept in check in part thanks to draws from the SPR. For the week ending October 30, 400,000 barrels of crude oil left the SPR to aid commercial inventories, bringing the total inventory held in the SPR down to 282.2 million barrels —a level that is 432 million barrels shy of maximum capacity. The generally accepted operational minimum for oil in the SPR is between 250-300 million barrels, below which the reserve may find it difficult to pump and process oil efficiently. US production for the week ending Oct 23 rose to 13.992 million bpd , up from 13.269 million bpd in the week prior, and up 348,000 bpd from a year ago. At 4:25 pm ET on Wednesday, Brent crude was trading down on the day at $104.32 (-0.43%). Brent is trading down roughly $10 per barrel from this time last week. WTI was also trading slightly up on the day, by $0.22 per barrel (+0.23%) at $97.24 , which is down roughly $3 per barrel since this time last week. Gasoline inventories rose by 1.427 million during the week ending October 30. In the week prior, gasoline inventories rose by 2.39 million barrels. In the week prior, gasoline inventories were 2% below the five-year average for this time of year, according to the latest EIA data. Distillate inventories fell by 270,000 barrels compared to the 380,000 barrels gained in the week prior. Distillate inventories were already 10% below the five-year average heading into this reporting period, the latest EIA data shows. Cushing inventory—the inventory kept at the delivery hub for the WTI Crude futures contract—gained 511,000 barrels after losing 453,000 barrels in the previous week. summary: Toronto-based i-80 maintained its 40,000–50,000 oz. outlook but flagged delayed access to high-grade ore.
body: I-80 Gold (TSX: IAU; NYSE: IAUX) expects annual production in the lower half of its forecast range after worker turnover slowed mining in Nevada, even as the company’s next underground operation approaches a year-end start. The stock dropped. Toronto-based i-80 maintained its 40,000–50,000 oz. outlook but flagged delayed access to high-grade ore at Granite Creek and a processing change that shifts some gold from the Archimedes mine into early 2027. Production mining at Archimedes and the refurbishment of the Lone Tree processing plant remain on schedule, i-80 said in its quarterly update Monday. “The contractor workforce has since been restored to previous staffing levels to support planned mining rates following an adjustment to contractor compensation structure,” chief operating officer Paul Chawrun said in the release. The setbacks highlight the operating demands behind i-80’s plan to lift annual gold output to 150,000–200,000 oz. starting in 2028. Its Lone Tree restart would allow the company to process its own refractory ore, which requires treatment to release gold trapped in sulphide minerals, and retain more of the margin now paid to third parties. I-80 shares fell 5.2% to $1.83 Tuesday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$1.6 billion ($1.1 billion). They’ve traded between $1.25 and $3.04 in the past year. I-80’s third-quarter net loss widened to $48.4 million, or 6¢ a share, from $41.9 million, or 5¢, as development and exploration expenses increased, according to Monday’s statement. Quarterly output fell 6% from a year earlier to 11,685 oz., while revenue edged higher to $32.7 million as stronger gold prices offset fewer ounces sold. I-80 had cash and cash equivalents of $411.4 million as of Sept. 30, down from $464.6 million three months earlier. National Bank Financial calculated potential liquidity of roughly $620 million including a conditional $100-million expansion of the gold-prepayment arrangement and about $109 million from the exercise of warrants whose exercise prices were below the share price. National Bank Financial mining analyst Don DeMarco maintained his outperform rating and C$4 target in a note Monday evening. Despite the near-term production weakness, development remained funded and on schedule, he said. Lone Tree remains the central investment in i-80’s growth plan. First gold is targeted for the fourth quarter of 2027 following a refurbishment budgeted at about $430 million. Labour costs are running 5%–10% above initial estimates, though they remain within the project contingency. About 44% of capital has been committed and 20% of contingency drawn, according to DeMarco. The contingency draw compares with roughly 10% cited in a development update last month, he noted. Payments on Lone Tree contracts are being made four to five months after commitments, against an originally assumed 30 days, moving expenditure into 2027, DeMarco said. Beyond Lone Tree, i-80 has moved Mineral Point ahead of the Granite Creek open pit and Cove underground project in its development sequence. The change concentrates spending on its largest growth project while reserving Cove as a later source of processing-plant feed. An Archimedes feasibility study and Mineral Point prefeasibility study are now expected in the second half of 2027, a modest shift from the previous mid-year targets, DeMarco noted. “In our view, continued execution at Granite Creek, Archimedes and Lone Tree can progressively de-risk the development pipeline and narrow the gap between asset value and market valuation,” he said. Staffing was already a concern last month during an analyst visit. Granite Creek’s mining contractor had about 100 employees against a target of roughly 120 amid strong competition for skilled workers in northern Nevada, SCP Resource Finance said in an Oct. 26 note. The mine had enough working areas to support higher output, but labour availability and the speed of the mining cycle were the constraints, SCP said. W

title: Will the Fed raise interest rates this year? Divided economists weigh in - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
body: The central bank has held interest rates steady five consecutive times. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh this week struck a combative tone about inflation, but the central bank opted against deploying its most powerful weapon: An interest rate hike . "The path to central bank heaven means delivering on our remit," Warsh told reporters in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday afternoon. "This is the right team to win the battle against high inflation." The remarks came minutes after the central bank issued its decision to hold interest rates steady for a fifth consecutive time, though pressure for a rate hike seemed to be building within its ranks. Three of the 12 members on the Fed's policymaking board voted in favor of a rate hike, marking the largest number of dissenters casting ballots in the same direction since 2016. After the announcement, economists appeared as divided as the policymakers, underscoring the uncertain prospects for a rate hike by the end of this year. Some analysts told ABC News they expect a rate increase as soon as the Fed's next meeting in September, pointing to risks posed by price increases as global oil shortage shows little sign of letting up. Others cast doubt on whether the Fed will raise rates at all over the remainder of 2026, noting an apparent willingness on the part of Warsh to let the market push borrowing costs higher without a nudge from the central bank. "Uncertainty and volatility are a feature and not a bug," Joseph Brusuelas, global economist at RSM, said in a note to investors about Warsh's stated preference that investors respond to economic events rather than Fed policy statements. "This has turned out to be anything but a boring and uneventful summer," Brusuelas added. The Iran war triggered a historic oil shortage that drove up fuel costs and catapulted inflation to a three-year high in May, the same month Warsh took the helm of the central bank. A preliminary peace agreement in June offered up some relief , but a burst of on-again, off-again fighting in recent weeks has caused crude prices to rise again. Elevated price increases pose a challenge for central bankers eager to beat back price hikes. In theory, the Fed could raise interest rates in an effort to cool off prices, but the move risks a slowdown of hiring. Fortunately, hiring has proven largely resilient, despite increased costs borne by shoppers and businesses. Odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in September stand at 63%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool , a measure of investor sentiment. Odds of a rate hike by the end of the year stand at 83%. "I do think we're going to see a rate hike. Maybe not at the next meeting but at some time in 2026," Rebel Cole, a professor of finance at Florida Atlantic University who formerly worked at the Federal Reserve, told ABC News. "Inflation won't come down until oil prices do. The Fed is boxed in." Some economists, by contrast, questioned whether the Fed would raise interest rates over the remainder of the year. The Fed holds little capacity to address inflation driven by supply shortages, such as the current oil shock, Brusuelas said. Higher interest rates would instead reduce demand as shoppers and businesses weather expensive borrowing costs. The Fed may instead expect inflation to fall once oil supply returns, Brusuelas said. "We think that the nature of the supply shock and the Fed's tendency to look through such shocks implies that the Fed has the space to keep the policy rate on hold," Brusuelas added. Warsh, meanwhile, has said he wants to let investors set the cost of borrowing in the market for short- and long-term bonds, instead of taking a strong hand himself through public statements or policy prescriptions. In a sense, that approach has worked, some economists said. The 30-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2007 on Wednesday, after the Fed issued its rate decision. title: TD Wealth® Insights: What Record Stocks and Higher Bond Yields are Telling Investors - TD Stories
body: The third quarter delivered sharply different outcomes across financial markets. Stocks reached record highs, while rising interest rates challenged bonds. Beneath the surface, strong artificial intelligence-related earnings, elevated energy prices and higher borrowing costs shaped performance and reinforced the importance of diversification, quality and a long-term perspective. The S&P 500 gained 2.3% during the quarter, but performance varied considerably across sectors. Energy, technology and health care led the market, while rate-sensitive areas such as utilities and real estate came under pressure. Small-cap stocks also struggled as higher energy prices and borrowing costs presented additional headwinds. International developed markets were roughly flat, while emerging markets experienced a modest decline. Fixed income faced a more challenging environment. Sharply higher yields pushed the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index down 3.5%, while credit sectors weakened and heavy issuance weighed on municipal bonds. Although the repricing created near-term losses, it also raised starting yields to more attractive levels, potentially improving future income and return opportunities. 1 Record stock prices and elevated bond yields may appear to send conflicting signals. In our view, both reflect an economy that has remained stronger than expected. Healthy corporate profits have continued to support equities, with earnings growth broadening across sectors. At the same time, bond yields have risen as inflation remains elevated, fiscal deficits increase, and investors adjust to higher interest-rate expectations. So far, corporate earnings growth has been strong enough to absorb the effects of higher interest rates, and we believe that bond yields should begin to moderate over the next year. Looking ahead, economic growth is expected to remain above 2% through the remainder of 2026 and in 2027, supported by fiscal policy, AI and business investment, and a resilient consumer. The labor market has also remained resilient and should continue to remain steady, with unemployment averaging near 4% through the end of 2027. Inflation remains the central challenge. Services inflation has been slow to cool, while tariffs and elevated energy prices have kept goods prices higher. Although these pressures are likely to gradually moderate over time, core inflation may remain sticky and above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target until late 2027 or early 2028. The Federal Reserve held rates steady in October and we currently expect them to raise rates once more in December. A subsequent pause, followed by gradual inflation improvement, could allow the Fed to begin cutting rates in the second half of 2027. The approaching midterm elections may increase market uncertainty, but we do not believe investors should reposition portfolios around a particular outcome. Election-related volatility has historically tended to fade once results provide greater clarity. Historically, markets have generally produced positive returns in the 12 months following midterm elections. 1 Economic growth and corporate earnings generally matter more to markets than which party controls Congress. Additionally, successfully investing around an election requires two correct decisions: predicting the outcome and anticipating how markets will respond. A comprehensive financial plan remains a more reliable foundation than a short-term political forecast. Overall, TD Wealth remains constructive on risk assets, with a modest preference for equities over fixed income. Healthy growth in corporate earnings, continued investment in AI and supportive fiscal policy provide a favorable backdrop for stocks. However, narrow market leadership and elevated valuations in some areas warrant a more selective approach. body: Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jumping 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock was up 8% in extended trading. Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter: Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement . Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius rallied earlier Tuesday and remained higher after AMD reported results. CEO Lisa Su said on the earnings call that she expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI growth to accelerate even faster than the company had projected 90 days ago. The company expects data center to drive the majority of its revenue and earnings growth. "We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year," Su said on the earnings call. AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But Intel's stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand . The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago. After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta 's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October. "Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work," Su said on the earnings call with analysts. AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI. AMD is also a major player in the weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm -based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research . AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago. For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount. AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. Meta, Microsoft , Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering. AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering . During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." title: This Under-the-Radar AI Infrastructure Stock Just Crushed Estimates and Raised Guidance - The Globe and Mail
AMD's Data Center Revenue Nearly Doubles as Q3 Results Top Estimates, Stock Climbs 7% - BigGo Finance
body: Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) delivered a third-quarter report that beat Wall Street on both the top and bottom lines, sending the chipmaker's shares up 7% in extended trading Tuesday as data center sales nearly doubled from a year earlier. The company posted adjusted earnings of $2.09 per share on revenue of $13.38 billion, according to CNBC. Analysts surveyed by LSEG had expected $1.95 per share on $13.09 billion. Revenue climbed 45% from $9.25 billion in the same period a year ago, coming in above the high end of AMD's own guidance range. The data center unit now accounts for 64% of total sales, up from 47% a year earlier, reflecting how thoroughly the AI buildout has reshaped AMD's business mix. Chief Executive Lisa Su said in a statement that she expects growth in data center processors to "accelerate further" and that the company is confident in its ability to sustain "very strong revenue growth and expanding profitability over the coming years." AMD's results landed just days after Intel Corp. (INTC) disclosed its own surge in data center revenue, up 78% in the quarter. But Intel's stock tumbled 29% on Friday as investors balked at soft guidance and questions about the company's capacity to fill orders. For the fourth quarter, AMD guided to roughly $17 billion in revenue, above the $16.2 billion consensus tracked by LSEG. The company projected a non-GAAP gross margin of 55%, a hair below the 55.3% average estimate compiled by StreetAccount. Growth is increasingly concentrated in data centers. Data center revenue rose 97% to $8.55 billion, and the segment's operating income more than doubled to $2.88 billion, lifting its operating margin to 34% from 25% a year earlier. The client and gaming segment remained a drag overall, but the weakness was concentrated in gaming. Segment revenue fell 8% year over year to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue dropped 40% to $773 million on lower semi-custom and graphics sales, while the client business, which houses PC processors, grew 7% to $2.9 billion on Ryzen mobile sales. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter, according to Counterpoint Research, as memory and other component costs climbed. The investment cycle behind that expansion is visible in cash flow. Free cash flow fell to $554 million from $1.53 billion a year earlier, while capital expenditures jumped 151% to $648 million. AMD's server CPUs have found a second wind with the spread of agentic AI applications, which rely on virtual machines that can run autonomously for hours. Demand from that corner of the market pushed the shares to a record in October. The stock is up about 125% this year, though it had lost 23% over the prior month during a sector-wide selloff tied to worries about AI spending before Tuesday's rally. Investors are focused on whether AMD's large accelerator commitments convert into revenue and margin rather than simply headlines. The company sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems under the Helios brand, competing directly with Nvidia Corp.'s (NVDA) Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin platforms. Meta Platforms Inc. (META) said last week that its Helios racks are running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in the social media company's equity offering. Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) plans to deploy Helios on Azure, with shipments expected to ramp through the fourth quarter and into 2027. Oracle Corp. (ORCL) said last week it will offer cloud services powered by AMD's next-generation EPYC processors, though no launch date has been disclosed. OpenAI is expected to bring Helios online this quarter. Meta has committed to deploying up to six gigawatts of AMD GPUs and holds warrants for as many as 160 million AMD shares tied to shipment and other milestones. OpenAI holds a similar warrant for up to 160 million shares, tied to deployments that could also reach six gigawatts. title: AMD shares jump 7% in extended trade after strong Q3 results, guidance, data center bet - CNBC TV18
body: Shares of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) jumped as much as 8% in extended trading on Tuesday, November 3, after the company's strong third quarter results, and an equally strong guidance for the ongoing quarter as well. Revenue for the quarter stood at $13.38 billion, higher than the estimate of $13.09 billion. On a year-on-year basis, the company's revenue grew by 45%. Earnings Per Share (EPS) stood at $2.09, higher than the $1.95 estimate. For the ongoing quarter, AMD expects $17 billion in revenue with a variation of 3% in either direction, comfortably higher than the average analyst estimate of $16.3 billion. AMD's MD & CEO Lisa Su said she expects the company's server revenue to double from last year in 2027, while the data center AI growth will accelerate even faster than what the company had projected three months prior. It is the data center business that will contribute to a majority of AMD's revenue and earnings growth in the future. During the quarter gone by, AMD's data center business contributed to 64% of the overall topline, from 47% earlier. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps, as they power virtual machines and can run for hours by themselves. It is this agentic demand that took AMD shares to a record high last month. Su expects demand to grow sharply in this segment as more agents are deployed to take on more complex work. Similar to Intel, AMD's PC chip sales fell 8% from last year, although it now is a smaller part of the business. Intel had earlier warned of a slowdown in the PC market globally, sending the stock lower by a record 29% in a single session. The company has also made a commitment to invest $5 billion in IPO-bound Anthropic. Su added on the earnings call that they plan on "substantially increasing" their supply over the next year. AMD shares ended 6.7% higher in extended trade at $516.32. The stock had closed 3.7% higher in regular trading on Tuesday before the results were announced after the bell. The stock is up 117% so far this year.
